Fast Sparse \(\alpha\)-Navigable Graph Construction with Improved Resource Augmentation

**Abstract**

Graph-based nearest neighbor search methods have surged in popularity in recent years. These methods are based on running greedy search on a directed graph constructed over a set of _n_ points, _x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_, endowed with some distance function. A common goal is to construct a search graph that has the \(\alpha\)-_navigability_ property, which ensures that greedy search returns provably good approximate nearest neighbors and converges in a small number of iterations. As the parameter \(\alpha\ge 1\) increases, accuracy improves, as does convergence rate, but there is a tradeoff: higher values of \(\alpha\) require the graph to have more edges, which increases both the data structure’s space and search time. This tradeoff has motivated the study of algorithms for constructing a _sparsest_ \(\alpha\)-_navigable graph_ for a given set of points.

In this work, we present improved algorithms for constructing \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs. For any point set and any distance function, we show how to compute an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph _G_ with a number of edges no more than _O_(log_n_) times that of the sparsest \((1+\varepsilon)\alpha\)-navigable graph. The algorithm runs in \(O(n^\omega log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) time, where \(\omega<2.372\) is the exponent of fast matrix multiplication and \(\Delta\) is the ratio between the largest and smallest pairwise distances in the input set. This result improves on recent work by Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten (SODA 2026), who achieve the same runtime, but are only competitive with the sparsest \(2(1+\varepsilon)\alpha\)- navigable graph. Since sparsity often increases rapidly with \(\alpha\) (typically \(\alpha\) is chosen \(\le 1.1\)) such a result can be significantly weaker than our bound. Previously, the best algorithm that could compete with the sparsest \((1+\varepsilon)\alpha\)-navigable graph required _O(n_<sup>2.5</sup>) time. Beyond our main result, we show that our techniques extend to the related problem of constructing sparse \(\tau\)-monotonic graphs, another popular target in nearest neighbor search. Moreover, we provide a fine-grained complexity analysis that suggests that improving the \(O(n^\omega)\) running time in our result is unlikely, or at least would require a very different algorithmic approach. This analysis is based on proving hardness results for problems related to _verifying_ whether a graph is navigable, which is a topic of independent interest.

## 1 Introduction

Nearest neighbor search has been a central problem in computer science for decades [4, 6, 7, 9-11, 23, 27, 29]. Given a dataset _P_={_p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p<sub>n</sub>_} together with a distance function \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\), the goal is to construct a data structure that can answer (approximate) nearest-neighbor queries: given _q_, return a \(p\in P\) that (approximately) minimizes _d(p,q_). Interest in this problem has recently surged due

<tbc>to its central role in modern AI systems, which often represent data using high-dimensional vector embeddings. Tasks such as semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation, recommendation, and clustering all require fast nearest-neighbor search over such vector representations \[8, 26, 30, 31, 41\].

Given the problem’s importance, many different methods have been proposed to solve approximate nearest neighbor search, including well-known and widely used methods like locality sensitive hashing \[2, 3, 20\], quantization-based inverted file indices \[17, 23, 24\], and tree-based methods \[7, 35\]. In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in a class of algorithms referred to as **_graph-based nearest neighbor search methods_**. Such methods include Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) Graphs \[33\], Vamana/DiskANN \[28, 40\], Navigating Spreading-out Graphs (NSG) \[16\], and more \[5, 6, 15, 18, 32, 34, 36, 37\]. Such methods offer state-of-the-art performance on a number of leading benchmarks and search competitions \[6, 37, 38\].

In graph-based methods, the core data structure used to support nearest neighbor search is a directed graph _G_=(_P,E_) with a node corresponding to every point in the dataset. A query _q_ is serviced by starting at some node in the graph, and greedily moving to the out-neighbor that is closest to _q_. The search continues in this way, terminating when no closer neighbor exists. Given the simplicity of this greedy search algorithm, a key differentiator between graph-based methods is how the search graph _G_ is constructed. How should the edges in _E_ be chosen to facilitate fast and accurate nearest-neighbor search?

## 1.1 \(\alpha\)-Navigable Graph Construction

While many different approaches have been employed to construct search graphs, **_navigability_** has been repeatedly identified as a desirable property for such graphs \[32, 40\]. A graph is **_navigable_** if, for every source point _s_ and distinct target point _t_ in _P_, the graph has an edge (_s,v_) where _d(v,t)\<d(s,t_), i.e. the source has an edge that leads closer to the target. On such a graph, a greedy traversal from any starting point in _P_ must converge to any query point, so long as that query is itself a member of _P_; at every step, the navigability property ensures that the traversal can make progress, until it lands on the query itself.

This basic property can be strengthened to \(\alpha\)**_-navigability_**, defined for any parameter \(\alpha\ge 1\). In this case, it is not sufficient that a source simply have an edge leading closer to each target: it must have an edge that shrinks the distance to a target by a multiplicative factor of \(\alpha\) or more. Formally, for each source-target pair _s,t_, there must be an edge (_s,v_) where \(d(v,t)<\frac{1}{\alpha}d(s,t)\).

\(\alpha\)-navigability is a powerful property. If _G_ has this property, then greedy search not only converges to any query in _P_, but it can be shown that it provides provably accurate approximate nearest neighbors for arbitrary queries. In particular, as long as the distance function _d_ is a metric, for any query _q_, greedy search will converge to a nearest neighbor whose distance from _q_ is no more than \(\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}\) times that of the query’s true nearest neighbor \[21\]. We obtain a better approximation for larger values of \(\alpha\).

Moreover, in addition to ensuring provably accurate results, \(\alpha\)-navigability ensures fast convergence. When \(\alpha>1\), we will converge to an \(\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}\)-approximate nearest neighbor in no more than

\(\lceil log_\alpha(\Delta_P)\rceil,\)

steps, where the **_aspect ratio_** \(\Delta_P\) of _P_, is the ratio between the largest and smallest pairwise distances in _P_. Moreover, search does not just converge for queries in _P_.

Fast convergence alone, however, does not govern the computation cost of graph-based nearest neighbor search. In particular, the cost of every search iteration scales with the number of out- neighbors of the current node. I.e., search is faster if _G_ is sparse. Graph sparsity also controls<tbc>

<tbc>the space complexity of the search data structure, an important consideration in applications. The importance of sparsity motivates the main algorithmic question considered in this paper:

**Problem 1.1** (Sparse \(\alpha\)-Navigable Graph Construction)**.** _Given a dataset P_={_p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p<sub>n</sub>}, distance function_ \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\)_, and_ \(\alpha\ge 1\)_, return an_ \(\alpha\)_-navigable graph G_=(_P,E_) _with as few edges as possible._

The study of this problem was recently initiated in \[12\] and \[25\]. While constructing the sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph is NP-hard, even for points in Euclidean space \[12\], an _O_(log_n_) approximation can be obtained in _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) time by reframing the problem as _n_ set cover instances (see 2.3 for more details). These recent papers improve this bound. For example, letting \(\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha\) denote the minimum number of edges in any \(\alpha\)-navigable graph for _P_, \[12\] presents an algorithm for constructing an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph with \(O(\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha logn)\) edges that runs in worst-case \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2.5})\) time.<sup>1</sup>

\[25\] gives an even faster algorithm in a **_resource-augmented_** setting. They present an \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega log(\Delta_P)/\varepsilon)\) time algorithm that computes an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph with \(O(\mathsf{OPT}_{2\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}logn)\) edges, where \(\varepsilon>0\) is any small constant and \(2\le\omega<2.372\) is the exponent of fast \(n\times n\) matrix multiplication. This result is resource-augmented bound because \(2\alpha(1+\varepsilon)>\alpha\), we have that \(\mathsf{OPT}_{2\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\ge\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha\).<sup>2</sup> Thus, the algorithm returns a graph whose sparsity is within an _O_(log_n_) factor of an objective larger than \(\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha\). Such an algorithm can yield a runtime improvement if \(\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha\in\widetilde{\omega}(n^{\omega-1}log(\Delta_P))\), as other algorithms exist which run in \(\widetilde{\widetilde{O}}(n\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha)\) time.

## 1.2 How much resource augmentation is too much?

While resource augmentation leads to a clear runtime advantage, reducing graph construction cost from roughly \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2.5})\) time to roughly \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega)\) time, it is natural to ask how much of a price is paid in terms of graph sparsity. In other words, **how much larger is** \(\mathsf{OPT}_{2\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\) **than** \(\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha\)**?**

In short, the answer is that the gap between these quantities can be substantial. When constructing \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs for real-world datasets, practitioners tend to set \(\alpha\) close to 1 (usually in the range \[1.0,1.2\]) \[33,34,39,40\]. \(\alpha\) is always chosen less than 2. Recalling that higher \(\alpha\) improves both accuracy and convergence rate, this suggests that even \(\mathsf{OPT}_2\le\mathsf{OPT}_{2\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\) is too large to be usable. Indeed it has been confirmed experimentally that, on many real-world datasets, as \(\alpha\) grows towards 2, the sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph becomes essentially complete.

One explanation for this is that, while not truly random, many modern high-dimensional vector embedding datasets exhibit properties of random points in Euclidean space. In particular, the majority of vectors are nearly orthogonal to each other, so distances between points tend to be similar. Indeed, in common embedding datasets, the aspect ratio is quite low, with the maximum pairwise distance no more than a small factor of the minimum. In an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph with \(\alpha>2\), any source-target pair requires an edge that gets at least 50% closer to the target. For common datasets, such an edge may simply not exist: the only option is to connect directly to the target. I.e., OPT<sub>2</sub> will be close to _n_<sup>2</sup>.

Given this, the goal of this work is to develop graph construction algorithms that enjoy the same efficient runtime as the method of \[25\], but without sacrificing so much on sparsity. In particular, instead of competing with \(\mathsf{OPT}_{2(1+\varepsilon)\alpha}\), ideally we would return a graph whose sparsity is competitive with the best \((1+\varepsilon)\alpha\)-navigable graph, where \(\varepsilon\) can be set arbitrarily close to zero.

<sup>1</sup>For the special case of \(\alpha=1\), this runtime can be further improved to \(\widetilde{O}(n^2)\), which is essentially optimal under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis \[12\]. We also note that for general \(\alpha\), the method actually runs in \(\widetilde{O}(min(n\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha,n^{2.5}))\), so can be faster than \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2.5})\) if \(\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha=o(n^{1.5})\). <sup>2</sup>Prior work uses the term **_bicriteria_** to refer to these algorithms. We prefer to use the term _resource-augmented_ since there are in fact not two criteria being optimized. Rather, we our goal is to return a graph whose size is competitive with the sparsest graph satisfying a slightly stricter set of constraints.

## 1.3 Our Contributions

The discussion above exposes a concrete gap between existing construction algorithms: one can obtain a strong sparsity guarantee with a running time of roughly \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2.5})\), or a faster \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) running time with resource augmentation that may make the resulting sparsity guarantee prohibitively weak. Our results largely close this gap. We first give an \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\)-time algorithm that reduces the resource augmentation from \(2\alpha(1+\varepsilon)\) to \(\alpha(1+\varepsilon)\). We then study the navigability- verification subroutine that forms the principal bottleneck in this algorithm, giving conditional lower bounds on improving or eliminating it.

### Improved resource augmented approximation algorithm

Our first result is an improvement of \[25\]’s resource augmented approximation algorithm, tightening the sparseness guarantee.

**Theorem 1.2.** _For any_ \(\varepsilon>0\)_, there exists a randomized algorithm that, given point set P, arbitrary distance function_ \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\)_, and_ \(\alpha>1\)_, constructs an_ \(\alpha\)_-navigable graph, with at most_

\(O\big(OPT_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}logn\big)\)

_edges,_<sup>3</sup> _where_ \(OPT_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\) _is the size of the sparsest_ \(\alpha(1+\varepsilon)\)_-navigable graph. The algorithm runs in_ \(\widetilde{O}\big(n^\omega\cdot log(\Delta_P)/\varepsilon\big)\) _time,_<sup>4</sup> _where_ \(\Delta_P\) _is the set’s aspect ratio._

The starting point for Theorem 1.2 is the observation that a sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph problem can be formulated as a combination of _n_ individual set cover problems. Since the \(\alpha\)-navigable constraint for a source-target pair (_s,t_) is satisfied by an edge (_s,v_) where \(d(v,t)<\frac{1}{\alpha}d(s,t)\), we can express a source point _s_ as a set cover problem where the elements to be covered are all targets \(t\neq s\). In this set cover instance, the sets correspond with potential outedges from _s_, with the set associated with edge (_s,v_) containing all targets _t_ where \(d(v,t)<\frac{1}{\alpha}d(s,t)\). Our main approach, then, is to efficiently solve these _n_ set cover instances.

\[25\] also makes this observation, but its \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega\cdot log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) time algorithm does not solve the set cover instances directly, instead adding edges through a geometric argument relying on triangle inequality. At a high level, the driving observation is that an edge from a source point _s_ to an intermediate point _v_ that approaches a given target by a factor of \(2\alpha\) can be replaced with an edge to some other point near _v_ and still approach the target by a factor of \(\alpha\). Thus, the authors add roughly \(OPT_{2\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\) edges and argue that these solve a large number of the source-target constraints from required for an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph. This is the source of the factor of 2 from their resource augmentation.

To eliminate the factor of 2, we replace this with a procedure that directly accesses and solves the underlying set cover instances. This not only comes with a tightening of the resource augmentation but also removes the requirement that the points live in a metric space. Unlike \[25\], our algorithm works on any symmetric distance function, without need for triangle inequality. We do, however, reuse a procedure from \[25\], which we detail in Section 2.5, that there is a small number of discrete pairwise distances among the points in _P_. To this end, we choose several fixed distance scales and round each distance to one of these, incurring up to a \((1+\varepsilon)\) distortion on all distances. Thus, we retain the \((1+\varepsilon)\) resource augmentation factor.

<sup>3</sup>The guarantee is actually slightly stronger: the constructed graph not only minimizes the total number of edges, but also individual degrees. That is, the out-degree of each point is within _O_(log_n_) of its lowest possible out-degree in any \(\alpha\)-navigable graph over _P_. <sup>4</sup>We assume \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\) takes _O_(1) time. More generally, if computing \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\) takes _O(T_) time, then our algorithm runs in \(\widetilde{O}\big(n^\omega\cdot log(\Delta_P)/\varepsilon\big)+O(n^2\cdot T)\) time. The same caveat applies to the prior works discussed in Section 1.1, which also take on an additional \(O(n^2\cdot T)\) cost for computing distances.

Finally, we show that the same framework extends to the related problem of constructing sparse \(\tau\)-monotonic graphs; see Section 3.3.

### Hardness of navigability verification.

A key component of our construction, inherited from \[25\], is a black-box procedure that determines which source-target \(\alpha\)-navigability constraints are satisfied by the edges currently in the graph. After distances are discretized, the constraints at each distance scale can be checked using one matrix multiplication. These matrix multiplications dominate the running time of our algorithm, so a substantially faster verification procedure would immediately yield a faster resource-augmented constructions.

This motivates us to study navigability verification as an independent algorithmic problem. We prove two hardness results. First, even when restricted to source-target pairs at a single fixed distance, \(\alpha\)-navigability verification is at least as hard as Boolean matrix multiplication: an \(n\times n\) Boolean matrix product can be computed using one call to the verification procedure and _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) additional time. Thus, bypassing matrix multiplication in our verification routine would require a corresponding breakthrough for Boolean matrix multiplication. Second, we consider exact verification over all undiscretized distances. We show that this problem is equivalent, up to polylogarithmic factors, to Boolean min-plus product. Combining this equivalence with a recent conditional lower bound for Boolean min-plus product \[14\], we show that, under the APSP conjecture, exact \(\alpha\)- navigability verification cannot be solved in \(O(n^{2.5-\delta})\) time for any constant \(\delta>0\). Together, these results suggest that both the matrix multiplication bottleneck and the use of resource augmentation are difficult to avoid within our framework.

## 1.4 Technical Overview and Prior Work

A first general answer for the question of how sparse a navigable graph can be made, and how efficiently such a graph can be constructed was given by \[13\]. They showed every _n_-point dataset admits a nontrivial sparse navigable graph, independent of the ambient dimension and without relying on metric structure. Their construction takes the union of a nearest-neighbor graph and a random graph, and in \(\widetilde{O}(n^2)\) time constructs a navigable graph with \(\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})\) edges. Equivalently, every point set admits a navigable graph of average degree \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n})\). This bound is essentially tight in the worst-case: for random points in _O_(log_n_)-dimensional Euclidean space, a navigable graph must have average degree \(\Omega(n^{1/2-o(1)})\) (with high probability).

This worst-case picture, however, does not capture the instance-by-instance structure of the problem. Many datasets may admit navigable graphs far sparser than the \(\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})\)-edge worst-case guarantee. Thus the more refined objective is not merely to construct some sparse navigable graph, but to approximate the sparsest navigable graph for the given instance. This instance-optimal viewpoint was subsequently developed \[12, 25\]. The key observation in both of these works is that the sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph problem decomposes into _n_ coupled set-cover instances, one for each source _s_. For a fixed source _s_, a candidate outgoing edge (_s,u_) covers exactly those targets _t_ for which _u_ gives a valid \(\alpha\)-progress step toward _t_. Thus, choosing the minimum out-neighborhood of _s_ is precisely a minimum set-cover problem over the set of targets _P_\\{_s_}. Solving these _n_ set-cover instances near-optimally yields a near-optimal sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph. In fact, it produces an even stronger approximation property: for every \(s\in P\), the out-neighborhood of _s_ is approximately the size of the minimum neighborhood of _s_ in any navigable graph. This set-cover formulation immediately yields an _O_(log_n_)-approximation to the optimum via the greedy set-cover algorithm, but a direct implementation takes cubic time even only to construct the sets explicitly.

The main algorithmic driver of \[12\] is a randomized simulation of the greedy algorithm, intended to solve each set cover instance without explicit constructions of the sets. At each step, a universe<tbc>

<tbc>element is sampled. Then, all sets covering the element are recorded. The amount of votes a set received is used as an estimator for its size, used to pick larger sets. This produces an algorithm that computes a _O_(log_n_)-approximation of the sparsest navigable graph in \(\widetilde{O}(n\cdot\text{OPT})\) time. Pairing this with clever preprocessing that exploits relationships between the different set cover instances reduces the running time for general \(\alpha\ge 1\) to \(\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{min}\{n\cdot\text{OPT},n^{2.5}\})\). For the case of \(\alpha=1\), i.e., navigable graphs, further dependencies can be exploited to produce a near-optimal \(\widetilde{O}(n^2)\) running time.

The work by \[25\] includes an algorithm that computes an _O_(log_n_)-approximation of the sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph in \(\widetilde{O}(n\cdot\text{OPT})\) time. It features the same core idea of a randomized simulation of the greedy algorithm seen in \[12\]. It also includes a potentially faster resource augmented approximation algorithm that runs in \(O(n^\omega\cdot\mathrm{log}(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) time, and computes an _O_(log_n_)-approximation of the sparsest \(2\alpha\cdot(1+\varepsilon)\)-navigable graph, where \(\varepsilon>0\) can be chosen arbitrarily, and \(\Delta\) is the aspect ratio of the point set. Observe that this is a weaker density guarantee as the sparsest \(2\alpha\cdot(1+\varepsilon)\)-navigable graph may be much denser than the sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph. This resource augmented approximation is largely comprised of two subroutines. The first subroutine covers a constant fraction of all uncovered source-target constraints, and the second subroutine is used to verify all satisfied constraints. The implementation of the first subroutine introduces the multiplicative 2 in the \(2\alpha\cdot(1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation. Further, for a fast implementation of the second subroutine, specifically by using fast matrix multiplication, distances are discretized, which introduces the multiplicative \((1+\varepsilon)\) approximation term.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Navigability and \(\alpha\)-Navigability

**Definition 2.1** (Navigable Graph)**.** _Given point set P and distance function_ \(d:P\times P\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^+\)_, we say that a directed graph G_=(_P,E_) _is_ navigable _if, for any source point_ \(s\in P\) _and target point_ \(t\in P\), \(s\neq t\)_, there exists some edge_ \((s,v)\in E\) _such that d(v,t)\<d(s,t). That is, s has an edge that, when taken, gets closer to t._

Equivalently, for every source _s_ and target _t_, there exists a directed path _p_<sub>0</sub>=_s,p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p<sub>k</sub>=t_ from _s_ to _t_ such that \(\forall i:d(p_{i+1},t)<d(p_i,t)\). That is for every source-target pair, there exists a monotone path from the source to the target, and thus the most basic form of greedy search will succeed. Navigability has been studied in the nearest-neighbor search literature for decades \[5, 12, 22, 25\].

While the definition of navigability only guarantees the convergence of basic greedy search for targets that are within _P_, recent work also shows that multiplicative approximation guarantees can be obtained for points outside of _P_ in an arbitrary metric when using Adaptive Beam Search, a variant of basic greedy search \[1\].

#### \(\alpha\)-Navigable graphs

A well-studied direct generalization of navigable graphs \[12, 21, 25, 28\], \(\alpha\)- Navigability requires not only that a monotone path between every source and target exists, but that the distance to the target shrinks at a multiplicative rate of \(\frac{1}{\alpha}\) at every step along the path.

**Definition 2.2** (\(\alpha\)-Navigable Graph)**.** _Given point set P and distance function_ \(d:P\times P\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^+\)_, and_ \(\alpha\ge 1\)_, we say that a directed graph G_=(_P,E_) _is_ \(\alpha\)-navigable _if, for any source point_ \(s\in P\) _and target point_ \(t\in P\), \(s\neq t\)_, there exists some edge_ \((s,v)\in E\) _such that_ \(d(v,t)<\frac{1}{\alpha}\cdot d(s,t)\).

A ubiquitous modern nearest-neighbor search algorithm, DiskANN \[28\] constructs graphs that are \(\alpha\)-navigable 5. While the definition of navigability maintains that every greedy search converges, \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs aim to ensure fast convergence by imposing a rate of progress. Further, recent work \[21\] shows that greedy search over \(\alpha\)-Navigable graphs always returns an approximate nearest neighbor \(\widetilde{p}\) with \(d(q,\widetilde{p})\le\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}\cdot min_{p\in P}d(q,p)\), even when \(q\notin P\). ## 2.2 Distance Access Model Our input is a set of points _P_={_p_1_,...,pn_} together with oracle access to a distance function \(d:P\times P\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). A query to the oracle returns the distance between two points in _O_(1) time. We otherwise treat the points and the distance function as black boxes; in particular, our algorithms do not require access to an explicit representation of the points. We make only two assumptions on the distance function. The first is that _d_ is symmetric, that is, _d(pi,pj_)=_d(pj,pi_).6 The second is that _d(pi,pj_) is 0 if _pi=pj_ and positive if \(p_i\neq p_j\). This is so that a point is its own nearest neighbor; otherwise, greedy traversal may not converge on a query even on a navigable graph. Notably, we do not require that _d_ is a metric. ## 2.3 Reducing Sparsest Navigable Graphs to Minimum Set Cover It has been observed independently by \[12, 25\], that the problem of constructing a sparse \(\alpha\)-navigable graph over a point set _P_={_p_1_,...,pn_} can be cast as a collection of _n_ coupled set cover instances, each with _n_-1 elements, and _n_-1 sets. Specifically, we have a single set cover instance for each point. The instance corresponding to point _pi_ involves covering all points \(p_k\neq p_i\), and has a set for every \(j\neq i\), denoted by \(S_{i\rightarrow j}\). \(S_{i\rightarrow j}\) contains every point _pj_ provides a greedy step towards when standing at _pi_, i.e., all points _pk_ such that \(d(p_j,p_k)<\frac{1}{\alpha}\cdot d(p_i,p_k)\). In other words, if we consider source-target \(\alpha\)-navigability constraints in which _pi_ is the source, \(S_{i\rightarrow j}\) contains all targets which corresponding constraints are satisfied by adding the directed edge (_pi,pj_). Observe that a set cover for this instance corresponds to an out-neighborhood for _pi_ that covers all \(\alpha\)-navigability constraints in which _pi_ is the source, and a minimum set cover corresponds to a minimum such out- neighborhood. Consequently, finding minimum set cover for all said instances produces a minimum navigable graph. The relationship between these different set cover instances was leveraged by \[12\] to produce efficient query access to these instances without explicitly constructing them, which we will review next. ## 2.4 Set Access Model and Efficient Query Access for Set Cover Under the distance access model described in Section 2.2, we can efficiently query the set cover instances induced by the problem of constructing a sparse navigable graph over _P_. In particular, within the set cover instance corresponding to _pi_, \[12\] showed that with _O(n_2log_n_) preprocessing, we can support the following three operations in constant time: \(\text{MemberOf}(p_k,S_{i\rightarrow j})\text{returns Yes if}p_k\in S_{i\rightarrow j}\text{and No otherwise.}\)
\(\text{FreqOf}(p_k)\text{returns the number of sets}S_{i\rightarrow j}\text{containing}p_k\text{.}\) 5Since the algorithm producing a strict \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs is too slow in practice, the authors of \[28\] propose a faster heuristic method, which is widely used. 6Technically, this is not strictly required since all distances during greedy traversal are computed against a common query point, so traversal converges even in the presence of asymmetric distances.

SetOf\((p_k,\ell\in[n])\) returns the \(\ell\)th set \(S_{i\rightarrow j}\) containing _p<sub>k</sub>_ (in some order), assuming \(\ell\le\mathrm{FreqOf}(p_k)\).

Suppose we fix the set cover instance, that is, we fix _i_. Supporting MemberOf queries is straightforward. By definition, \(p_k\in S_{i\rightarrow j}\) if and only if \(d(p_j,p_k)<\frac{1}{\alpha}\cdot d(p_i,p_k)\), which can be determined by only two distance accesses.

To support the other two queries, we first preprocess a **_distance-based permutation matrix_**. This is an \(n\times n\) matrix \(\Pi\) where the _i_th row stores the sorted order of all points by increasing distance from _p<sub>i</sub>_. That is, \(p_{\Pi_{i,j}}\) is the _j_th closest point to _p<sub>i</sub>_. This matrix can be constructed in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>log_n_) time by simply sorting each row.

Using the permutation matrix, we observe that, because \(p_k\in S_{i\rightarrow j}\Longleftrightarrow d(p_j,p_k)<\frac{1}{\alpha}\cdot d(p_i,p_k)\), all of the sets \(S_{i\rightarrow j}\) containing _p<sub>k</sub>_ are associated with the closest points to _p<sub>k</sub>_ and can therefore be found within some prefix of the _k_th row of \(\Pi\). We can find the length of the prefix by binary search on row _k_ for the last point _j_ satisfying \(d(p_j,p_k)<\frac{1}{\alpha}d(p_i,p_k)\). We can precompute these prefix lengths for all instances _i_ and targets _p<sub>k</sub>_ in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>log_n_) time total, then perform a simple lookup of these prefix lengths to answer FreqOf queries. SetOf queries follow the same principle; the \(\ell\)th set containing _p<sub>k</sub>_ is simply \(S_{i\rightarrow\Pi_{k,\ell}}\).

From this point on, we assume we have access to these three operations. We state this as a lemma.

**Lemma 2.3** (due to \[12\])**.** _Given a sparsest_ \(\alpha\)_-navigable graph construction problem specified by an input point set P and distance function_ \(d:P\times P\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^+\)_, there exists a data structure which supports_ MemberOf, FreqOf_, and_ SetOf _queries for the induced set cover instances in O_(1) _time. This data structure is constructed in O(n_<sup>2</sup>log_n_) _time and requires O(n_<sup>2</sup>) _space._

## 2.5 Batched Verification of Navigability Constraints via Matrix Multiplication

As in \[25\], a key component of our new algorithm for constructing sparse \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs is a routine for using fast matrix multiplication to verify the \(\alpha\)-navigability of a graph. Concretely, given a graph over _P_, we’d like to identify which source-target \(\alpha\)-navigability constraints are satisfied. We first describe how to verify all constraints at a single distance scale, then use distance discretization to verify all constraints.

**Lemma 2.4** (due to \[25\])**.** _Let G_=(_P,E_) _be a directed graph,_ \(\alpha\ge 1\)_, and r\>_0_. In_ \(O(n^\omega)\) _time, we can identify every pair_ (_s,t_) _such that there exists some edge_ \((s,v)\in E\) _satisfying d(v,t)\<r._

_Proof._ Let _A_ be the adjacency matrix of _G_, and define the matrix \(B^{(r)}\in\{0,1\}\) by

\(B_{j,k}^{(r)}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
1 & \text{if}d(p_j,p_k)<r \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.\)

We construct _B_<sup>(_r_)</sup> using _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) distance queries and compute the matrix product _C_<sup>(_r_)</sup>=_AB_<sup>(_r_)</sup>. For any (_i,k_), \(C_{i,k}^{(r)}>0\) if and only if there exists some _j_ such that \((p_i,p_j)\in E\) and _d(p<sub>j</sub>,p<sub>k</sub>)\<r_. Consequently, we can identify all pairs described in the lemma above by scanning through _C_<sup>(_r_)</sup> and outputting (_p<sub>i</sub>,p<sub>k</sub>_) whenever \(C_{i,k}^{(r)}>0\).

Constructing the matrices and inspecting the product take _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time, while computing the product takes \(O(n^\omega)\) time. Since \(\omega\ge 2\), the total running time is \(O(n^\omega)\).

The preceding lemma applies only to pairs at one particular distance. Applying this separately to up to \(\Theta(n^2)\) distinct distances is too expensive. We therefore group distances into geometrically increasing scales. For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), define the distance scales \(r_\ell=d_{min}(1+\varepsilon)^\ell\) for \(\ell=0,\dots,\lceil log_{1+\varepsilon}(\Delta)\rceil\), where \(d_{min}=min_{p\neq q}d(p,q)\). We now round each pairwise distance in _P_ down to the nearest scale \(r_\ell\), that is, we assign each distance \(x\in[d_{min},d_{max}]\) to the largest scale \(r_\ell\) satisfying \(r_\ell\le x\). Consequently, there are only \(O(log_{1+\varepsilon}(\Delta))=O(log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) distinct distances, and each new distance differs from its original distance by no more than a factor of \((1+\varepsilon)\). Let \(\rho(x)\) denote the rounded distance for a distance _x_.

We now define the verification procedure used throughout this paper.

**Lemma 2.5** (Batched verification)**.** _Given P, a directed graph G_=(_P,E),_ \(\alpha\ge 1\)_, and_ \(0<\varepsilon\le 1\)_, there is a procedure,_ \(VerifyNav(G,\alpha,\varepsilon)\)_, which runs in_

\(O\left(n^\omega\left(1+log_{1+\varepsilon}\Delta\right)\right)\)

_time and returns a set_ N(_G_) _of source-target pairs that_

1. _Includes all_ (_s,t_) _pairs where no edge_ \((s,v)\in E\) _satisfies_ \(d(v,t)<\frac{1}{\alpha}d(s,t)\)<tbc>

_2._ _Excludes all_ (_s,t_) _pairs where some edge_ \((s,v)\in E\) _satisfies_ \(d(v,t)<\frac{1}{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}d(s,t)\)

_Equivalently, if_ \(\mathcal{U}_\beta(G)\) _denotes the set of unsatisfied_ \(\beta\)_-navigability constraints, then_

\(\mathcal{U}_\alpha(G)\subseteq\mathcal{N}(G)\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}(G).\)

_Proof._ Recall from Lemma 2.4 that we can identify in \(O(n^\omega)\) time the exact set of (_s,t_) pairs where an edge \((s,v)\in E\) satisfies _d(v,t)\<r_.

We execute this procedure on the distance scales \(r^\ell/\alpha\) for \(\ell=0,\dots,\lceil log_{1+\varepsilon}(\Delta)\rceil\). Thus, we compute, for each distance scale \(r^\ell\), the set of all (_s,t_) pairs where some \((s,v)\in E\) satisfies \(d(v,t)<r^\ell/\alpha\). Now take any (_s,t_) pair. Recall that its rounded distance \(\rho(d(s,t))\) matches some distance scale \(r^\ell\). For that \(r^\ell\), consult whether some \((s,v)\in E\) satisfies \(d(v,t)<r^\ell/\alpha\). If not, return (_s,t_). We claim that doing this over all (_s,t_) pairs returns all pairs whose \(\alpha\)-navigability constraint is not satisfied and no pairs whose \(\alpha(1+\varepsilon)\)-navigability constraint is satisfied.

First, suppose some (_s,t_) pair’s \(\alpha\)-navigability constraint is not satisfied. That is, no (_s,v_) edge satisfies \(d(v,t)<\frac{1}{\alpha}d(s,t)\). Since \(\rho(d(s,t))\le d(s,t)\), it must also hold that no (_s,v_) edge satisfies the even stronger condition of \(d(v,t)<\frac{1}{\alpha}\rho(d(s,t))\). Thus, (_s,t_) is returned.

Second, suppose some (_s,t_) pair’s \(\alpha(1+\varepsilon)\)-navigability constraint is satisfied. That is, there is some edge, \((s,v^*)\in E\), where \(d(v^*,t)<\frac{1}{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}d(s,t)\). Since rounded distances are less than a \((1+\varepsilon)\) factor off from true distances, it follows that \(\rho(d(s,t))\ge\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon}d(s,t)\). Substituting \(d(s,t)\le(1+\varepsilon)\rho(d(s,t))\) yields that \(d(v^*,t)<\frac{(1+\varepsilon)}{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\rho(d(s,t))\le\frac{1}{\alpha}\rho(d(s,t))\). Thus, (_s,t_) is not returned.

Thus, we have shown that the set of returned source-target pairs satisfies the properties listed in the above lemma. Finally, the entire procedure takes _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time to check whether to return each pair, as well as \(O(log_{1+\varepsilon}(\Delta))=O(log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) calls to the procedure from Lemma 2.4, taking \(O(n^\omega log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) time total.

## 3 Fast Resource Augmented Sparsest \(\alpha\)-Navigable Graphs

In this section, we prove our main positive result. Recall from Section 2.3 that for each source point \(s\in P\), choosing the outgoing neighbors of _s_ is exactly a set cover problem: each possible edge (_s,v_)<tbc>

<tbc>covers the targets _t_ for which \(d(v,t)<\frac{1}{\alpha}d(s,t)\). Thus, constructing a sparse \(\alpha\)-navigable graph amounts to solving _n_ set cover instances, one for each possible source.

A direct greedy set cover implementation is too slow. Across all sources, there are _n_ set cover instances, each with _n_-1 candidate sets and _n_-1 elements. Explicitly materializing all sets already takes \(\Omega(n^3)\) time and space in the worst case. \[12\] circumvents this cost by avoiding building these sets explicitly. However, it incurs the cost of repeatedly updating the set of uncovered targets. For a source _s_, these updates can take \(\widetilde{\Omega}(n\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha(s))\) time, and summing over all sources gives the \(\widetilde{\Omega}(n\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha)\)-type bottleneck of prior approaches without resource augmentation.

Our main idea is to separate the tasks of proposing a cover for a set of uncovered points and applying that cover to remove those points. Locally, for each source _s_, we use a voting procedure to choose a batch of promising outgoing edges. Globally, after many such edges have been added across many sources, we use fast matrix multiplication (VerifyNav) to recompute which source- target constraints remain uncovered. Thus, the expensive materialization step is not performed after each selected edge, but only after a whole batch of updates. We will show that, for each set cover instance, each batch of edges added covers a constant fraction of the remaining constraints, so only _O_(log_n_) such global updates are needed. This is similar to the approach taken by \[25\], which also sought to repeatedly cover a constant fraction of constraints, but the method we use to achieve this bears closer resemblance to an algorithm described in \[19\], which computes covers over subsamples of a larger set cover instance.

Recall that the VerifyNav procedure requires rounding distances into a small number of geometric buckets, after which it can no longer distinguish between distances within a bucket, up to a \((1+\varepsilon)\) multiplicative factor apart. It can, however, distinguish constraints that are definitely unsatisfied at parameter \(\alpha\) from constraints that are definitely satisfied at the stronger parameter \(\alpha(1+\varepsilon)\). This is why our sparsity bound is measured against the optimal \(\alpha(1+\varepsilon)\)-navigable graph: the residual instances we continue to solve may erroneously contain points falsely believed by VerifyNav to be unsatisfied at parameter \(\alpha\), and it may not be until the graph is \(\alpha(1+\varepsilon)\)-navigable before it correctly indicates that the graph is fully \(\alpha\)-navigable.

For clarity, we have the following local notation. For \(\beta\ge 1\) and source \(s\in P\), let

\(\mathsf{OPT}_\beta(s)=min\{|\mathcal{C}|:\mathcal{C}\subseteq P\backslash\{s\}\text{and}\forall t\in P\backslash\{s\},\exists v\in\mathcal{C}\text{such that}d(v,t)<d(s,t)/\beta\}\) (1)

Equivalently, \(\mathsf{OPT}_\beta(s)\) is the minimum out-degree needed at _s_ to satisfy all \(\beta\)-navigability constraints whose source is _s_. The theorem below gives a per-source guarantee, and therefore also implies the corresponding global edge bound of Theorem 1.2 by summing over all sources.

**Theorem 3.1.** _Let P be a set of n points with distance function d and aspect ratio_ \(\Delta\)_, and let_ \(\alpha\ge 1\)_. For any_ \(\varepsilon>0\)_, there is a randomized algorithm running in_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) _time that constructs an_ \(\alpha\)_-navigable graph over P such that, with high probability, every point_ \(s\in P\) _has out-degree_ \(\le O(logn)\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}(s)\).

Before giving the algorithm, we spell out the two ingredients that are combined in the proof.

## Voting as approximate greedy set cover

The procedure VoteCover, introduced in \[12\], can be viewed as a fast randomized simulation of the standard greedy set cover algorithm. The standard greedy algorithm achieves a log_n_ approximation, but naively applied, leads to _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) time to find a near-optimal \(\alpha\)-navigable graph. Given a source _s_ and a set \(U\subseteq P\backslash\{s\}\) of currently uncovered targets, VoteCover repeatedly samples uncovered targets from _U_. A sampled target _t_ casts a vote for every candidate edge (i.e., set) (_s,v_) that would cover it, namely every _v_ satisfying \(d(v,t)<d(s,t)/\alpha\). Sets with many votes are good estimators for sets covering many currently<tbc>

uncovered targets, so the algorithm adds the set with the most number of votes (after ∼log_n_ samples), then explicitly updates _U_ by removing every target now covered by that set.

This explicit update of _U_ is the bottleneck. Without efficient access to the points covered by a given edge, this is done in VoteCover through a full scan over _U_. Because the size of _U_ does not shrink quickly enough with each new edge, this takes \(\Omega(n\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha(s))\) total time in the worst case. Summed over all sources, this is too expensive for the desired \(n^\omega\)-time bound - recalling that \(\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha=\sum_{s=1}^n\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha(s)\), we would obtain a running time of \(\Omega(n\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_\alpha)\). It was shown in \[12\] that a preprocessing step could reduce this cost to amortized \(\widetilde{O}(n)\) per source by shrinking the initial size of _U_ when \(\alpha=1\), but the approach does not extend in general to \(\alpha>1\).

### Batched verification by matrix multiplication

To reduce the cost of updating _U_, our algorithm introduces a second main ingredient: the verification routine of Section 2.5.

Suppose first that the distances between input points take only _W_ distinct values. This can be enforced by rounding each continuous distance to the nearest discrete distance scale. For a fixed distance scale, the set of constraints satisfied by the current graph can be found by one Boolean matrix multiplication, as reviewed in Section 2.5. Repeating over all _W_ scales gives a verification procedure running in \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega W)\) time. By rounding distances geometrically to powers of \((1+\varepsilon)\), we may take \(W=O(log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\); this is the source of both the \((1+\varepsilon)\) resource augmentation slack and the \(log(\Delta)/\varepsilon\) factor in the running time.

Our algorithm uses this routine as a global replacement for the expensive scans inside VoteCover. Rather than updating the uncovered set after each selected edge, we let every source add a batch of edges, and then use a VerifyNav routine to refresh all their uncovered sets simultaneously. The rest of this section formalizes this batched voting procedure. In Section 3.1, we define PartialVoteCover, which covers a constant fraction of a given residual instance. In Section 3.2, we show how to obtain a fast overall runtime by running this partial cover routine for all sources in parallel and using VerifyNav to update the residual constraints between batches.

## 3.1 Partial Cover

Here we introduce PartialVoteCover (Algorithm 3.1), which differs from VoteCover in one fundamental way: given a set _U_ of uncovered elements, PartialVoteCover is only asked to cover at least |_U_|/2 elements of _U_ rather than all of them. The way this manifests itself is that PartialVoteCover constructs a cover over a sample _K_ of _U_ instead of over _U_ directly. Controlling the size of the sample allows us to bound both the amount of work we do and the number of sets in the partial cover. This approach bears similarity to sampling methods used in prior work on set cover algorithms in sublinear-time models of computation \[19\].

The voting process is largely as in VoteCover. Each uncovered sample casts votes for the sets containing it until some set receives _c_ln_n_ votes, where _c_ is a fixed constant. That set is then added to the cover, and the points that voted for it revert their votes for other sets. This repeats until all samples have voted, and the cover is returned.

### 3.1.1 Correctness and success probability

We now prove that PartialVoteCover covers at least half of _U_ with high probability. First, we note a few simple properties of the output of PartialVoteCover.

**Observation 3.2.** _PartialVoteCover returns a partial cover_ C _containing no more than_ \(\frac{C}{c}\cdot\mathsf{opt}\) _sets._

**Algorithm 3.1** PartialVoteCover \((\mathcal{S}_\beta,U,\mathsf{opt},C,c)\)

**Input:** A set system \(\mathcal{S}_\beta\), a set of elements _U_ to cover, a guess `opt` of \(\mathsf{OPT}_\beta(s)\), and constants _C,c\>_0.

**Output:** A partial cover \(\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_\beta\) that covers at least |_U|/_2 elements from _U_.

2: \(K\leftarrow\) a multiset of \(C\cdot\mathsf{optln}n\) independent samples from _U_

3: **while** \(K\neq\varnothing\) **do**

4: \(v\leftarrow\) element sampled uniformly at random from _K_

5: \(K\leftarrow K\backslash v\)

6: **if** \(v\in\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal{C}}S\) **then** \(\triangleright\) Check if any sets containing _v_ (via SetOf) are in C

7: **continue**

8: \(V\leftarrow V\unknown\{v\}\)

9: \(S^*\leftarrow\mathrm{argmax}_{S\in\mathcal{S}_\beta}|V\cap S|\)

10: **if** \(|V\cap S^*|\ge c\mathrm{ln}n\) **then**

11: \(\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{C}\cup\{S^*\}\)

12: \(V\leftarrow V\backslash S^*\triangleright\) Remove all votes cast by elements covered by _S_<sup>∗</sup>, including duplicates

13: **return** C

_Proof._ Each set added to the cover in PartialVoteCover consumes _c_ln_n_ voters. That is, the _c_ln_n_ samples that voted for that set are removed from _V_ and their votes eliminated from all sets. Since the initial number of samples in _K_ is \(C\cdot\mathsf{optln}n\), the algorithm can successfully find a set exceeding the vote threshold at most \(\frac{C\mathsf{optln}n}{c\mathrm{ln}n}=\frac{C}{c}\cdot\mathsf{opt}\) times.

**Observation 3.3.** _Before or after any iteration of the while-loop of Algorithm 3.1, every set_ \(S\in\mathcal{S}\) _satisfies_ \(|V\cap S|<c\mathrm{ln}n\).

_Proof._ We prove this by induction. It is trivially true at the start of the algorithm since _V_ is empty. Now assume that it holds at the start of a given iteration, i.e. \(|V\cap S|<c\mathrm{ln}n\) for all \(S\in\mathcal{S}\). Observe that on each iteration, _V_ grows by at most one element, _v_, so any \(|V\cap S|\) likewise grows by at most one, up to a maximum of _c_ln_n_. If any sets _S_ now satisfy \(|V\cap S|=c\mathrm{ln}n\), then Line 10 triggers, and one such set is subtracted from _V_ . However, all satisfying sets share the element _v_, so this subtraction necessarily removes at least one element, _v_, from all their intersections with _V_ . Therefore, all sets once again satisfy \(|V\cap S|<c\mathrm{ln}n\).

**Observation 3.4.** _Of the points initially in K, the partial cover_ C _returned by PartialVoteCover leaves fewer than_ \(c\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_\beta(s)\mathrm{ln}n\) _uncovered._

_Proof._ At the end of PartialVoteCover, the points initially in _K_ that are not covered by C are exactly those that remain in _V_ . By definition of \(\mathsf{OPT}_\beta(s)\), the elements of \(V\subseteq U\) can be fully covered by at most \(\mathsf{OPT}_\beta(s)\) sets, i.e. by the optimum cover of _U_. However, by Observation 3.3, each of the sets in this optimum cover contains fewer than _c_ln_n_ of the elements in _V_ . Thus, the number of points in _V_ is bounded by \(|V|<c\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_\beta(s)\mathrm{ln}n\) via the Pigeonhole Principle.

Using these observations, we now prove that an appropriate choice of the constants _C_ and _c_ ensures that PartialVoteCover covers at least half of the elements in _U_ with high probability.

**Lemma 3.6.** _Consider running PartialVoteCover on the set cover instance corresponding with source s, and let_ FreqOf _be as defined in Section 2.4 for that instance, i.e. for a given element v,_ FreqOf(_v_) _is the number of sets in the instance which contain v.
