_Proof._ The runtime bottlenecks in PartialVoteCover are Lines 6 and 10. Recall from Section 2.4 that we can answer in constant time any of the following queries: (1) MemberOf, which answers whether a given set contains a given element; (2) FreqOf, which returns the number of sets containing a given element; and (3) SetOf, which returns the _i_th (according to some arbitrary order) set containing a given element. We will just assume we have access to these primitives, but we refer back to Section 2.4 for a description of how these primitives can be supported in the set cover instances of a sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph instance.

## Line 6: check if an element has been covered.

We maintain C in a hash table. To check if element _v_ is covered by C, we scan over all possible sets that contain _v_ (by finding the number of sets with FreqOf and iterating over them with SetOf) and, for each one, check if it is contained in the hash table representing C. We return **true** if any such set is in C. We do one constant-time membership query per set containing _v_, so \(\le\mathrm{FreqOf}(v)\) per sample _v_, and \(\le\sum_{v\in K}\mathrm{FreqOf}(v)\) in total.

## Line 9: find the set with the most votes.

For each \(S\in\mathcal{S}\), we maintain the intersection \(V\cap S\) in a hash table. We update all of these hash tables any time _V_ is modified. _V_ is modified on Lines 8 and 12.

Line 8 adds _v_ to _V_ . The only intersections \(V\cap S\) that change are those where \(v\in S\). We can find these by calling SetOf operations on _v_. For each such set _S_, we do a single constant-time insertion into its \(V\cap S\) hash table, for a maximum of \(\sum_{v\in K}\mathrm{FreqOf}(v)\) across all voters.

Line 12 runs after a set _S_<sup>∗</sup> has been added to C. It subtracts _S_<sup>∗</sup> from _V_ . The elements we must remove from _V_ are exactly those in the hash table for \(V\cap S^*\). Thus, we iterate over \(V\cap S^*\), and for each element _v_ in it, we must remove _v_ from all \(V\cap S\) hash tables. But note that the sets _S_ where \(v\in V\cap S\) are exactly those where \(v\in S\). We can iterate through these by calling SetOf operations on _v_. For each of these, we do a single constant-time hash table deletion. We can bound the total number of deletions by observing that any _v_ can only be removed from _V_ once. Since each such _v_ is removed from FreqOf(_v_) hash tables, we perform a maximum of \(\sum_{v\in K}\mathrm{FreqOf}(v)\) deletions over the course of PartialVoteCover.

Having bounded the cost of maintaining the hash tables, how do we efficiently identify the largest (Line 9) in order to evaluate the condition on Line 10? We first note that it is only necessary to identify the most voted set if the condition passes. We know from Observation 3.3 that at the start of each loop iteration, the condition must be false. Thus, it can only become true when a hash table grows. It follows that it is sufficient to check, whenever a hash table grows due to Line 8, whether it now has size _c_ln_n_, and set _S_<sup>∗</sup> to that set if so. Therefore, we can satisfy Lines 9 and 10 in time proportional to the number of hash table insertions, which is no more than \(\sum_{v\in K}\mathrm{FreqOf}(v)\).

It follows that PartialVoteCover runs in \(O(\sum_{v\in K}\mathrm{FreqOf}(v))\) time.

## 3.2 \(\alpha\)-Navigable Graphs in Batches

Having established that PartialVoteCover covers at least half of the elements in _U_ when given a valid parameter opt, we now describe how we use it to build a full \(\alpha\)-navigable graph. It is easy to see that if we can cover a constant fraction of _U_, then we can do so again to cover another constant fraction of the remainder, and that we will eventually cover all of _U_ after at most log<sub>2</sub>(|_U_|) calls to PartialVoteCover. Our full algorithm follows this general strategy.

**Algorithm 3.2** BatchedVoteCover \((P,\alpha,\varepsilon,C,c,\gamma)\)

**Input:** A set _P_ of _n_ points and constants \(\alpha\ge 1\), \(\varepsilon,C,c>0\), and integer \(\gamma\ge 0\).

**Output:** A graph _G_.

1: \(G,U\leftarrow\) an array of _n_ sets

2: \(Q\leftarrow P\)

3: **for** \(\mathsf{opt}\in\{2^1,2^2,2^3,\dots\}\) **do**

4: **for** \(p_i\in Q\) **do**

5: \(G[i]\leftarrow\) a set of optln_n_ elements sampled from _P_

6: \(U[i]\leftarrow P\backslash\{p_i\}\backslash\bigcup_{p_j\in G[i]}S_j\)

7: **for** \(t\in[\mathrm{log}_2n+\gamma]\) **do**

8: **for** \(p_i\in Q\) **do**

9: \(G[i]\leftarrow G[i]\cup\mathsf{PartialVoteCover}(\{S_{i\rightarrow j}^{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}:j\in[n]\},U[i],\mathsf{opt},C,c)\)

10: \(\mathcal{N}\leftarrow\mathsf{VerifyNav}(G,\alpha,\varepsilon)\)

11: **for** \(p_i\in Q\) **do**

12: \(U[i]\leftarrow\{t:(i,t)\in\mathcal{N}\}\)

13: **if** \(U[i]=\emptyset\) **then** \(Q\leftarrow Q\backslash\{p_i\}\)

14: **if** \(Q=\emptyset\) **then**

15: **return** _G_

However, it is not so simple. If we wish to run PartialVoteCover on the remaining uncovered elements, we need to identify which elements of _U_ are still uncovered. This is difficult because, whereas we have efficient access to the sets containing a given element, we do not have efficient access to the elements contained in a given set. The naive approach of iterating over _U_ and removing any elements covered by some set in C takes too long (\(\Omega(n\cdot|\mathcal{C}|)\) time).

This is where we employ the VerifyNav procedure described in Section 2.5. Recall that given a graph, VerifyNav takes \(O(n^\omega\cdot\mathrm{log}(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) time to return a list N of pairs (_s,t_) that includes any pair whose \(\alpha\) constraint is not satisfied and excludes any pair whose \(\alpha(1+\varepsilon)\) constraint is satisfied.

Thus, we can use VerifyNav to identify all _U_ that remain uncovered for a given set cover instance. Upon obtaining a partial set cover C for the set cover instance corresponding to point _p<sub>i</sub>_, we add to _G_ the edges (_p<sub>i</sub>,p<sub>j</sub>_) for all \(S_{i\rightarrow j}\in\mathcal{C}\). Then, we run VerifyNav on _G_ to obtain N, and the remaining uncovered points are all those _t_ where \((p_i,t)\in\mathcal{N}\). But note that using VerifyNav in this way to materialize the remainder of _U_ for only a single set cover instance is wasteful. Instead, we run a single VerifyNav to materialize the uncovered points for all set cover instances simultaneously.

That is, we execute PartialVoteCover on each set cover instance, obtaining a partial cover for each. We add the edges corresponding to those covers to an accumulated graph. Then, we run VerifyNav on the graph to list all remaining unsatisfied constraints. We run PartialVoteCover again on these remaining constraints. This process repeats roughly _O_(log_n_) times, which we know to be sufficient because each round covers a constant fraction of constraints. An important caveat<tbc>

<tbc>with this approach is that PartialVoteCover only succeeds in covering enough constraints when given a parameter `opt` close enough to its true optimum cover size \(\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\). To accomplish this, we run the entire procedure over doubling guesses of \(\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\), ensuring that we find a serviceable value `opt` within \(\mathrm{log}(\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)})\) attempts.

Only one detail remains. Recall from Lemma 3.6 that the running time of PartialVoteCover is proportional to the sum of all frequencies of the elements it samples. It is not hard to see that, across all set cover instances, the frequency of an element is large (roughly _n/_2) on average. Thus, we attach an additional preprocessing step alongside each guess `opt` which serves to bound the frequency of each element. Namely, we add `opt`ln_n_ random edges to each point. This covers a large number of constraints - in particular, it covers all constraints with high frequency. After having added these random edge, we use VerifyNav to identify the targets that remain uncovered, all of which have low frequencies.

This full algorithm, BatchedVoteCover, is laid out in Algorithm 3.2. It remains to be shown that BatchedVoteCover returns a near-optimally-sparse \(\alpha\)-navigable graph, and that it does so in \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega\mathrm{log}(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) time.

## 3.2.1 Approximation factor

Given that PartialVoteCover covers a constant fraction of the unsatisfied constraints for a given set cover instance, it is easy to see that BatchedVoteCover must successfully solve that set cover instance on or before the first iteration where `opt` exceeds the true optimal cover size for that instance.

**Observation 3.7.** _Given sufficiently-large constants C and c, as well as constant_ `opt` _satisfying_ \(\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}<\mathsf{opt}\le 2\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\)_, BatchedVoteCover (Algorithm 3.2) covers U in no more than_ \(\mathrm{log}n+\gamma\) _calls to PartialVoteCover with probability_ \(\ge 1-O(1/n^{\gamma-1})\)_, for any constant_ \(\gamma\).

_Proof._ If a call to PartialVoteCover covers at least half of _U_, we’ll say this call was "successful". By Lemma 3.5, each call to PartialVoteCover is successful with probability at least 1-1_/n_ given adequate constants _C_ and _c_. All points in _U_ are covered after no more than \(\lceil\mathrm{log}_2n\rceil+1\) successful calls. Thus, if we call PartialVoteCover \(\lceil\mathrm{log}_2n\rceil+\gamma\) times, we can only fail to cover _U_ if the unsuccessful calls number at least \(\gamma\).

By a union bound over the possible sets of \(\gamma\) unsuccessful calls, the failure probability of BatchedVoteCover is at most<tbc>

\(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\lceil\mathrm{log}_2n\rceil+\gamma}{\gamma}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^\gamma\le\left(\frac{e(\lceil\mathrm{log}_2n\rceil+\gamma)}{\gamma n}\right)^\gamma.\)

<tbc>In particular, for any constant \(\gamma\), this failure probability is

\(O\left(\frac{1}{n^{\gamma-1}}\right).\)

A bound on the size of the adjacency list constructed for a given point follows directly from Observation 3.2.

**Lemma 3.8.** _For a given point whose set cover instance has optimal cover size_ \(\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\)_, Batched- VoteCover constructs an adjacency list of size_ \(O(\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\mathrm{log}n)\) _with probability_ \(\ge 1-O(1/n^{\gamma-1})\).<tbc>

_Proof._ Because Algorithm 3.2 processes opt in increasing guesses of doubling magnitude, there must be some iteration where \(\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}<\mathsf{opt}\le 2\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\). If _p<sub>i</sub>_ is still unsolved (i.e. contained in _Q_) by this point, then by Observation 3.7, it will be solved on this iteration with probability at least \(1-1/n^{\gamma-1}\). Thus, by Observation 3.2, with probability \(\ge 1-1/n^{\gamma-1}\), _p<sub>i</sub>_ is removed from _Q_ having received at most \(\frac{C}{c}\cdot\mathsf{opt}\cdot(log_2n+\gamma)\le\frac{2C}{c}\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\cdot(log_2n+\gamma)\) edges from PartialVoteCover.

Thus, the final adjacency list of _p<sub>i</sub>_ is the union of \(\mathsf{optln}n\le 2\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}lnn\) random sets assigned by Line 5 and \(\le\frac{2C}{c}\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}\cdot(log_2n+\gamma)\) edges returned by PartialVoteCover. Combining these yields a total of \(O(\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}logn)\) edges.

Applying a union bound over all _n_ set cover instances, all adjacency lists are within an _O_(log_n_) factor of optimal with probability \(\ge 1-1/n^{\gamma-2}\).

## 3.2.2 Running Time

We now consider the running time of Algorithm 3.2.

While Lemma 3.5 establishes that BatchedVoteCover successfully solves each set cover instance within log(OPT) attempts, efficiently executing this procedure requires carefully bounding the time spent processing votes. Recall from Lemma 3.6 that PartialVoteCover spends time proportional to the sum frequency of all sampled elements. To achieve our desired running time, introduce a randomized preprocessing step to each set cover instance to limit the maximum number of sets containing any uncovered element.

**Lemma 3.9** (Frequency Bounding via Random Sets)**.** _Suppose we add a collection_ R _of_ optln_n sets chosen uniformly at random to the cover for p<sub>i</sub>. Let U be the set of elements remaining uncovered. With high probability, no element in U is contained in more than O(n/_opt) _sets._

_Proof._ Consider an element _p_ that is contained in at least \(\lambda\cdot n/\mathsf{opt}\) sets for some constant \(\lambda\). The probability that a single randomly chosen set covers _p_ is at least \(\frac{\lambda\cdot n/\mathsf{opt}}{n}=\frac{\lambda}{\mathsf{opt}}\). If we sample optln_n_) random sets, the probability that _p_ is not covered by any of them is at most

\(\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{\mathsf{opt}}\right)^{\mathsf{optln}n}\le exp(-\lambda lnn)\le\frac{1}{n^\lambda}\)

for an arbitrarily large constant \(\lambda\). Taking a union bound over all elements ensures that all high- frequency elements are covered with probability \(\ge 1-1/n^{\lambda-1}\), leaving only elements contained in _O(n/_opt) sets in _U_.

With the frequency of the uncovered elements bounded, we can efficiently execute the voting process inside PartialVoteCover. Since BatchedVoteCover adds optln_n_ outneighbors to each point _p<sub>i</sub>_, it follows that with probability \(\ge 1-1/n^{\lambda-2}\) (union bounding across all set cover instances), any uncovered target in any instance is contained in fewer than \(\lambda\cdot n/\mathsf{opt}\) sets. We now apply this directly to Lemma 3.6 to achieve the following result:

**Corollary 3.10.** _The execution of PartialVoteCover once for each active set cover instance in BatchedVoteCover takes_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^2)\) _total time._

Finally, we can bound the total running time of BatchedVoteCover.

**Lemma 3.11.** _The execution of BatchedVoteCover takes_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\) _time._

_Proof._ From Corollary 3.10, we know that one execution of PartialVoteCover on each set cover instance, after having bounded the frequency each target by means of adding random edges, takes _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time. We follow this with a call to VerifyNav, which takes \(O(n^\omega log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)\). This dominates the _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time for the calls to PartialVoteCover, as \(\omega\) is necessarily at least 2. We perform this combination of these PartialVoteCover and VerifyNav up to \(logn+\gamma\) times for a given choice of `opt`, ensuring that any active set cover instance _s_ where `opt` is sufficiently close to \(\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}(s)\) completes. Finally, we run this on up to log_n_ values of `opt` before guaranteeing that `opt` is sufficiently close to \(\mathsf{OPT}_{\alpha(1+\varepsilon)}(s)\) for every _s_ at least once. Therefore, the total running time of BatchedVoteCover is \(O(n^\omega(log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)log^2n)\).

The combination of Lemma 3.11 and Lemma 3.8 yields Theorem 3.1.

## 3.3 Extension to \(\tau\)-Monotonic Graphs

Although we have presented our algorithm in terms of \(\alpha\)-navigability, the underlying set cover and batched verification framework is not specific to multiplicative progress. We briefly observe that the preceding framework also applies to the construction of sparse \(\tau\)-monotonic graphs \[12, 36\]. For \(\tau>0\), a directed graph _G_=(_P,E_) is \(\tau\)_-monotonic_ if, for every pair of distinct points \(s,t\in P\), either \((s,t)\in E\), or there exists an edge \((s,v)\in E\) such that

\(d(v,t)<d(s,t)-\tau.\)

Thus, each step makes additive, rather than multiplicative, progress toward the target. The direct- edge alternative is necessary when \(d(s,t)\le\tau\), since in this case no point can satisfy the displayed inequality.

As with \(\alpha\)-navigability, selecting the out-neighbors of each source _s_ is a set cover problem. For each potential edge (_s,v_), define

\(T_{s\rightarrow v}=\{t\in P\backslash\{s\}:v=t\text{or}d(v,t)<d(s,t)-\tau\}.\)

The MemberOf, FreqOf, and SetOf operations from Section 2.4 continue to be supported in constant time after _O(n_<sup>2</sup>log_n_) preprocessing. In particular, for a fixed source _s_ and target _t_, the points _v_ satisfying \(d(v,t)<d(s,t)-\tau\) form a prefix of the points sorted by distance from _t_. The length of this prefix can be found by binary search and stored for every pair (_s,t_). The possible additional set \(T_{s\rightarrow t}\), corresponding to the direct edge (_s,t_), is handled separately.

The other change is that distance discretization is additive. By rescaling the distance function and \(\tau\), assume without loss of generality that the minimum nonzero pairwise distance is 1, so the maximum pairwise distance is \(\Delta\). We use the additive scales \(r_\ell=\ell\epsilon\) for \(\ell=0,\dots,\left\lceil\frac{\Delta}{\epsilon}\right\rceil\) and round each distance _x_ down to \(\rho(x)=\epsilon\left\lfloor\frac{x}{\epsilon}\right\rfloor\). Consequently,

\(x-\epsilon<\rho(x)\le x,\)

and there are \(O(\Delta/\epsilon)\) distance scales.

The corresponding VerifyNav procedure performs one matrix multiplication for each scale. At scale \(r_\ell\), in the notation of Lemma 2.4, we define<tbc>

\(B_{j,k}^{(\ell)}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
1, & j=k\text{or}d(p_j,p_k)<r_\ell-\tau, \\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>The diagonal entries account for direct edges. For a pair (_s,t_) whose distance rounds to \(r_\ell\), we report the constraint as unsatisfied if the corresponding entry of \(AB^{(\ell)}\) is zero. If \(\mathcal{U}_\eta(G)\) denotes the set of unsatisfied \(\eta\)-monotonicity constraints, the resulting set \(\mathcal{N}_\tau(G)\) satisfies

\(\mathcal{U}_\tau(G)\subseteq\mathcal{N}_\tau(G)\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{\tau+\epsilon}(G).\)

Indeed, rounding down cannot cause an unsatisfied \(\tau\)-constraint to be removed, while any constraint satisfied with additive progress \(\tau+\epsilon\) remains satisfied after its source-target distance is rounded down by less than \(\epsilon\). The procedure uses \(O(\Delta/\epsilon)\) matrix multiplications and therefore runs in \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega\Delta/\epsilon)\) time.

We may now apply BatchedVoteCover without further modification.

**Corollary 3.12.** _Let P be a set of n points with aspect ratio_ \(\Delta_P\)_, after normalizing its minimum nonzero pairwise distance to_ 1_. For every_ \(\tau\ge 0\) _and_ \(0<\epsilon\le 1\)_, there is a randomized algorithm running in_<tbc>

\(\widetilde{O}\left(n^\omega\frac{\Delta_P}{\epsilon}\right)\)

<tbc>_time that constructs a_ \(\tau\)_-monotonic graph G such that, with high probability, every_ \(s\in P\) _has out- degree at most_ \(O(\mathsf{OPT}_{\tau+\epsilon}(s)logn)\)_, where_ \(\mathsf{OPT}_{\tau+\epsilon}(s)\) _is the minimum out-degree required at s in any_ \((\tau+\epsilon)\)_-monotonic graph. Consequently,_

\(|E|\le O(logn)\cdot\mathsf{OPT}_{\tau+\epsilon}.\)

_Proof._ The analysis of BatchedVoteCover uses only constant-time access to MemberOf, FreqOf, and SetOf, together with a verification procedure whose output lies between the constraints unsatisfied at the desired parameter and those unsatisfied at the resource-augmented parameter. The set-access construction and the additive version of VerifyNav above provide these properties for parameters \(\tau\) and \(\tau+\epsilon\), respectively. The remainder of the proof of Theorem 3.1 applies unchanged.

The change from a logarithmic to linear dependency on \(\Delta_P\) in the running time when transitioning from \(\alpha\)-navigability to \(\tau\)-monotonicity is not surprising, as this reflects the increase in number of relevant distance scales from \(O(log_\alpha(\Delta_P))\) to \(O(\Delta_P/\tau)\). In contrast to \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs, which guarantee a logarithmic search convergence of \(O(log_\alpha(\Delta_P))\) steps, \(\tau\)-monotonic graphs likewise inherit a linear bound of \(O(\Delta_P/\tau)\) steps to converge.

## 4 Hardness

This section addresses two natural questions about the algorithms from the previous sections.

1. Can the running time of the resource augmented algorithm be improved? The main bottleneck is the subroutine that, at a fixed distance scale _d_<sub>0</sub>, lists all source-target pairs (_s,t_) whose \(\alpha\)-navigability constraints become satisfied after the newly added edges are inserted. In our current implementation, this subroutine is based on fast matrix multiplication and runs in \(O(n^\omega)\) time. Is there a substantially faster implementation?<tbc>

2. Can one eliminate the discretization step and obtain a more efficient exact single-criterion algorithm? More precisely, can one efficiently test, in the original metric, which \(\alpha\)-navigability constraints are satisfied by the current edge set? Any \(O(n^{2.5-\varepsilon})\)-time algorithm for this task, for a fixed constant \(\varepsilon>0\), would improve upon the current worst-case running time of the best known single-criterion algorithm.<tbc>

We formalize the corresponding testing problems and prove hardness results that answer both questions negatively.

**Definition 4.1.** _Let G_=(_P,E_) _be a directed graph, let d be a metric on P, let_ \(\alpha>1\)_, and let d_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0_. The_ single-scale \(\alpha\)-navigability testing problem _asks to report all pairs_ \((s,t)\in P\times P\) _such that d(s,t_)=_d_<sub>0</sub> _and there exists_ \(u\in P\) _with_

\((s,u)\in E\text{\textit{and}}d(u,t)\le\frac{1}{\alpha}d(s,t).\)

Question (1) asks whether one can avoid the bottleneck of matrix multiplication in solving this problem. Lemma 4.3 answers this question in the negative, showing that a reduction exists in the opposite direction, and that this problem is essentially equivalent to Boolean matrix multiplication.

**Definition 4.2.** _Let G_=(_P,E_) _be a directed graph, let d be a metric on P, and let_ \(\alpha>1\)_. The_ \(\alpha\)-navigability testing problem _asks to report all pairs_ \((s,t)\in P\times P\) _such that there exists_ \(u\in P\) _with_

\((s,u)\in E\text{\textit{and}}d(u,t)\le\frac{1}{\alpha}d(s,t).\)

Question (2) asks whether any \(O(n^{2.5-\varepsilon})\)-time implementation exists, as such an implementation would improve upon the state of the art single-criterion approximation. Corollary 4.9 answers this question in the negative by demonstrating APSP-hardness.

**Lemma 4.3.** _There is a reduction from Boolean matrix multiplication on two_ \(n\times n\) _matrices to single-scale_ \(\alpha\)_-navigability testing that uses one oracle call and O(n_<sup>2</sup>) _additional time._

_Proof._ Let \(A,B\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\). We construct an instance of single-scale \(\alpha\)-navigability testing as follows.

Let \(P=S\unknown U\unknown T\), where _S_={_s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>n</sub>_}, _U_={_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>n</sub>_}, and _T_={_t_<sub>1</sub>_,...,t<sub>n</sub>_}.

We first define a metric _d_ on _P_. Let _H_ be the undirected weighted graph on vertex set _P_ containing the following edges:

• for every \(i,j\in[n]\), an edge {_s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_} of weight 1;<tbc>

• for every \(k,j\in[n]\) with _B<sub>k,j</sub>_=1, an edge {_u<sub>k</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_} of weight \(1/\alpha\).

Let _d_ be the shortest-path metric of _H_.

Next, define a directed graph _G_=(_P,E_) by adding the edge (_s<sub>i</sub>,u<sub>k</sub>_) to _E_ if and only if _A<sub>i,k</sub>_=1.

We claim that one call to the single-scale \(\alpha\)-navigability testing oracle with parameter _d_<sub>0</sub>=1 suffices to compute the Boolean product _AB_.

First observe that in _H_, for every \(i,j\in[n]\), the direct edge {_s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_} has weight 1. This edge realizes the shortest-path distance, since alternative path from _s<sub>i</sub>_ to _t<sub>j</sub>_ has length greater than 1, as there are no direct edges between _S_ and _U_. Hence, _d(s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_)=1.

Therefore, for every \(i,j\in[n]\), the oracle reports (_s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_) if and only if there exists \(k\in[n]\) such that<tbc>

\((s_i,u_k)\in E\Longleftrightarrow A_{i,k}=1\text{and}d(u_k,t_j)\le\frac{1}{\alpha}\cdot d(s_i,t_j)=\frac{1}{\alpha}.\)

<tbc>Further note, for every \(k,j\in[n]\),

\(d(u_k,t_j)\le\frac{1}{\alpha}\Longleftrightarrow B_{k,j}=1,\)

because the only possible path in _H_ of weight \(\le\frac{1}{\alpha}\) between _u<sub>k</sub>_ and _t<sub>j</sub>_ in _H_, is the direct edge (_u<sub>k</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_) which is present if and only if _B<sub>k,j</sub>_=1. Overall, a pair (_s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_) is reported if and only if there exists \(k\in[n]\) such that _A<sub>i,k</sub>=B<sub>k,j</sub>_=1.

As a first step towards the proof of Corollary 4.9 we define the problem of Boolean min-plus product and prove that it has equivalent running time to \(\alpha\)-navigability testing up to polylogarithmic factors.

**Definition 4.4.** _Let M be an_ \(n\times n\) _matrix over_ \(\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\)_, and let N be an_ \(n\times n\) _Boolean matrix. Their_ Boolean min-plus product _is the matrix M⋆N defined by_

\([M\star N]_{i,j}=min\{M_{i,k}:N_{k,j}=1\},\)

_with the convention that the minimum over the empty set is_ \(+\infty\).

Equivalently, one may regard _N_ as a matrix over \(\{0,\infty\}\), replacing each 1 by 0 and each 0 by \(\infty\), and then take the usual min-plus product.

This is a problem that has been used as a subroutine to compute node-weighted APSP in previous works by Chan, Yuster, and Abboud et al most recently (see "All-Pairs Shortest Paths with Few Weights per Node " for more details). It’s hardness was studied in the recent "Universe Reduction for APSP: Equivalence of Three Fine-Grained Hypotheses", which demonstrated APSP-hardness.

**Lemma 4.5.** _\[Lemma 6.3 from Universe Reduction for APSP: Equivalence of Three Fine-Grained Hypotheses\] For every_ \(\varepsilon>0\)_, there does not exist an_ \(O(n^{2.5-\varepsilon})\) _algorithm for Boolean min-plus product on_ \(n\times n\) _matrices, unless the APSP conjecture is falsified._

For the purpose of proving \(\alpha\)-navigability testing is equivalent to Boolean min-plus product computation, we define an intermediate problem.

**Definition 4.6.** _Let_ \(A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) _and let_ \(B,C\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}\)_. The_ Boolean min-plus threshold testing problem _asks to report all pairs_ \((i,j)\in[n]\times[n]\) _such that_

\(min\{B_{k,j}:A_{i,k}=1\}\le C_{i,j},\)

_again with the convention that the minimum over the empty set is_ \(+\infty\).

**Lemma 4.7.** _Boolean min-plus product and Boolean min-plus threshold testing are equivalent up to polylogarithmic overhead. More precisely, if one of the two problems on_ \(n\times n\) _matrices can be solved in time T(n), then the other can be solved in time_ \(\widetilde{O}(T(n)+n^2)\).

_Proof._ We first reduce Boolean min-plus product to threshold testing.

Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}\) and \(N\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\), our goal is to compute _M⋆N_. For each row _i_, replace the entries of _M_ by their ranks within that row. Formally, define \(R\in[n]^{n\times n}\) by

\(R_{i,k}=\big|\{k'\in[n]:M_{i,k^\prime}\le M_{i,k}\}\big|.\)

Then, for every _i,j_, the value \[_R⋆N_\]_<sub>i,j</sub>_ is exactly the rank, within row _i_, of the minimum entry among the columns _k_ with _N<sub>k,j</sub>_=1, which makes recovering _M⋆N_ from _R⋆N_ straight forward in \(\widetilde{O}(n^2)\) time.

It therefore suffices to compute _R⋆N_, and this can be done using _O_(log_n_) calls to the threshold- testing oracle by parallel binary search on all entries simultaneously. More precisely, a threshold matrix _C_ is formed, and a search space for each coordinate is maintained (initialized to \[_n_\]). At each step, we query threshold testing on (_N<sup>T</sup>,R<sup>T</sup>,C<sup>T</sup>_). Following this call, for each pair _i,j_ we learn whether:<tbc>

\(min\{[R^T]_{k,i}=R_{i,k}:[N^T]_{j,k}=N_{k,j}=1\}\le[C^T]_{j,i}\Longleftrightarrow[R\star N]_{i,j}\le C_{i,j}\)

Based on the answer, for each _i,j_ we update the search space and _C<sub>i,j</sub>_ accordingly before the next query. Observe that the entries of \([R\star N]\) are in \([n]\cup\{\infty\}\) and thus the searches converge in _log(n_) steps.

Conversely, suppose we are given an oracle for Boolean min-plus product, and let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) and \(B,C\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}\) be an instance of threshold testing. Compute _D_=(_B<sup>T</sup>⋆A<sup>T</sup>)<sup>T</sup>_. Then, for every _i,j_,

\(D_{i,j}=min\{B_{k,j}:A_{i,k}=1\}.\)

Hence we can obtain the answer by comparing _D<sub>i,j</sub>_ with _C<sub>i,j</sub>_ entrywise.

We next relate threshold testing to \(\alpha\)-navigability testing.

**Lemma 4.8.** _Boolean min-plus threshold testing and_ \(\alpha\)_-navigability testing have equivalent running times - if one of the two can be solved in T(n_) _time, the other can be solved in T(n_)+_O(n_<sup>2</sup>) _time._

_Proof._ We begin with the reduction from \(\alpha\)-navigability testing to Boolean min-plus threshold testing.

Let _G_=(_P,E_) be a directed graph on _P_={_v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>n</sub>_}, and let _d_ be a metric on _P_. Define matrices \(A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) and \(B,C\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}\) by<tbc>

\(A_{i,k}=1\Longleftrightarrow(v_i,v_k)\in E,B_{k,j}=d(v_k,v_j),C_{i,j}=\frac{1}{\alpha}d(v_i,v_j).\)

<tbc>Then, for every _i,j_, we have \(min\{B_{k,j}:A_{i,k}=1\}\le C_{i,j}\) if and only if there exists _k_ such that

\((v_i,v_k)\in E\text{and}d(v_k,v_j)\le\frac{1}{\alpha}d(v_i,v_j),\)

which is exactly \(\alpha\)-navigability constraint for (_v<sub>i</sub>,v<sub>j</sub>_).

For the converse direction, let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) and \(B,C\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}\) be an instance of Boolean min- plus threshold testing. Let _S_={_s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>n</sub>_}, _U_={_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>n</sub>_}, and _T_={_t_<sub>1</sub>_,...,t<sub>n</sub>_}, and set \(P=S\unknown U\unknown T\).

Define a directed graph _G_=(_P,E_) by: \((s_i,u_k)\in E\) if and only if _A<sub>i,k</sub>_=1.

We now define a metric on _P_. Let \(W>\alpha max_{i,j}C_{i,j}+max_{k,j}B_{k,j}\). Let _H_ be the undirected weighted graph on _P_ containing the following edges:

• for every \(k,j\in[n]\), an edge {_u<sub>k</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_} of weight _W+B<sub>k,j</sub>_;<tbc>

• for every \(i,j\in[n]\), an edge {_s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_} of weight \(\alpha\cdot(W+C_{i,j})\).

Let _d_ be the shortest-path metric of _H_.

We claim that, for all _k,j_, _d(u<sub>k</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_)=_W+B<sub>k,j</sub>_, and, for all _i,j_, \(d(s_i,t_j)=\alpha W+\alpha C_{i,j}\). Indeed, each of these values is realized by a direct edge. Any alternative path from _u<sub>k</sub>_ to _t<sub>j</sub>_ uses at least two edges between _U_ and _T_ or two edges between _S_ and _T_ and therefore has weight at least 2_W\>W+B<sub>k,j</sub>_. Likewise, any alternative path from _s<sub>i</sub>_ to _t<sub>j</sub>_ has at least one edge connecting _S_ and _T_ and at least one edge connecting _U_ and _T_ and therefore has weight at least \(\alpha\cdot W+W>\alpha\cdot(W+C_{i,j})\).

Therefore, for every _i,k,j_,

\(d(u_k,t_j)\le\frac{1}{\alpha}d(s_i,t_j)\Longleftrightarrow W+B_{k,j}\le W+C_{i,j}\Longleftrightarrow B_{k,j}\le C_{i,j}.\)

It follows that the \(\alpha\)-navigability oracle reports (_s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>j</sub>_) if and only if there exists _k_ such that

\(A_{i,k}=1\text{and}B_{k,j}\le C_{i,j},\)

which is exactly the threshold-testing condition.

Combining Lemmas 4.5, 4.7 and 4.8 yields the following corollary.

**Corollary 4.9.** _For every constant_ \(\varepsilon>0\)_, there does not exist an_ \(O(n^{2.5-\varepsilon})\) _algorithm for_ \(\alpha\)_- navigability testing unless the APSP conjecture is falsified._
